E0889.summary: Direct, self-evident knowing, which Atwood treats as the evidence and end of all rational proof and the highest human certainty.
E0889.body: Atwood's own term for direct, self-evident knowing. She holds that “intuition is the evidence and end of every rational proof” [II.1 ¶33], and that “Intuitive faith is certain beyond all doubt, and needs no proof beyond itself” [II.1 ¶34]. On her account it is the highest certainty open to a human being.

E0890.summary: The level of life reached by cutting off the sensuous life; dissolving the sensuous reaches the intuitional, called divine.
E0890.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says: “You cut off the sensuous life and get into the intuitional” [APP ¶176]. Dissolving the sensuous life is said to reach the intuitional, which she calls divine. A reader linked it with the “medial life” of [APP ¶182], but that identity is inferred from the parallel, not stated in the text.

E0891.summary: The reversal of nature's ordinary order: Atwood calls it our present state, a requirement for perfect manifestation, and reason turning back on itself.
E0891.body:
Atwood uses the word in three related ways.

- **Our condition.** In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “Our present state is one of inversion.” [APP ¶45]
- **A requirement of the work.** The ordinary order of nature's procedure has to be reversed, and this lies beyond ordinary art and nature: the work proceeds “by a real experimental inversion” [I.2 ¶22], since “the order of natural procedure ought to be introverted for a true and perfect manifestation” [I.2 ¶27].
- **Reason turning back on itself.** Logic “becomes bounded about its own inversion” [III.2 ¶67], while the experiment actually carries the inversion out. Followed strictly, both lead to the First Source [III.2 ¶67].

The text does not say whether these are one process seen from different sides.

E0892.summary: The true worker of the work, according to a quoted Adept: the secret incubation of the Spirit of God upon nature.
E0892.body: A quoted Adept speaks here: “The work is performed by an invisible Artist; for there is a secret incubation of the Spirit of God upon nature” [IV.2 ¶18]. The invisible Artist is thus identified with the secret incubation of the Spirit of God upon nature, which is the real agent behind the work.

E0893.summary: The inner hand of which the outward hand is the image and clothing; it works effects according to what it has attained.
E0893.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says: “The hand outward is an image of the invisible hand, its clothing” [APP ¶177]. The invisible hand works its effects according to what it has attained.

E0894.summary: In Bohme's account, the agent that prepares the Antimonial Spirit, also called the spiritual air of Antimony.
E0894.body: Bohme is quoted here. The Invisible Mercury prepares the Antimonial Spirit. It works when condensed in its vehicle, and its operation brings the three principles into harmony [II.1 ¶21]. Identity: “the invisible Universal Mercury, or spiritual air of Antimony” [II.1 ¶21].

E0895.summary: Dutch adepts, father and son, who are said to have worked successfully; Atwood gives their works as references.
E0895.body: Atwood names the Isaacs (J. I. Hollandus and I. Hollandus) as Dutch adepts, father and son, who are said to have worked the art successfully [I.1 ¶58]. She gives their works, *de Lapide Philosophico* and *Opera Universalia*, as references [I.1 n63].

E0896.summary: Cited twice: for the overflowing of the dark power, and for gradual purifying and perfecting.
E0896.body:
Atwood cites Isaiah twice.

- Isaiah, Chap. 8, verse 8 illustrates how the dark power overflows at this stage of the work: “He shall overflow the channels, and go over all the banks” [III.1 ¶60, III.1 n65].
- Isaiah 38:13 supports gradual purifying and perfecting: “Line upon line, Precept upon precept” [IV.3 ¶39, IV.3 n19].

E0897.summary: The goddess Atwood identifies with nature, Minerva, Athena and the Wisdom under inquiry, and the name of the Matter once it becomes intelligent and convertible to every form.
E0897.body:
**In Apuleius (quoted).** Isis appears to Lucius and names herself: “call me by my true name, Queen Isis” [II.4 ¶17]. She calls herself nature: “I, who am nature, the parent of all things” [II.4 ¶17]. She is also queen of the elements, the one goddess “whose one divinity the whole orb of the earth venerates under a manifold form, by different rites and a various of appellations” [II.4 ¶17]. Among those appellations are Pessinuntica, Cecropian Minerva, Paphian Venus, Diana Dyctynna, Stygian Proserpine, Ceres, Juno, Bellona, Hecate and Rhamnusia.

**Atwood's identifications.** The Sphinx stood in “the vestibule of Isis, who is the same with Minerva and that Wisdom we are investigating” [III.1 ¶5]. So Isis is equated with Minerva and with the Wisdom that is the subject of the inquiry.

**In the fable and the work.** In the fable, Isis gathers Osiris's scattered members: “but Isis, recollecting, hides them in a chest” [III.1 ¶53]. In the work, the Lunar Vulcan plays her part. It tempers Typhon and reconciles the opposed principles, which then circulate with her in equilibrium [III.1 ¶63]. She is “as Isis in the Mysteries, where she is also called Athena” [III.1 ¶63]. That second name is given “to express that self-motion and intelligence with which this Spirit is endowed” [III.1 ¶63].

**Name of the Matter.** After the process described in [III.3 ¶61], the Matter is endowed with understanding, can be converted into any Form, and is the pre-existent mother of all. “Then she is Isis, the Divine I Am” [III.3 ¶62]. She is also “by the Greeks called Myrionymous, or the goddess with a thousand names” [III.3 ¶62]. Yet “As respects herself, she is Nothing” [III.3 ¶62].

All of these are Atwood's statements except the Apuleius passage, which she quotes.

E0898.summary: A pairing Atwood uses to illustrate reason constantly seeking her true Hypostasis.
E0898.body: Atwood uses the pair as an image: reason constantly seeks her true Hypostasis “as Isis for Osiris” [II.3 ¶46].

E0899.summary: Isis of the old mythology, used to illustrate the divine beauty pursued and the Goddess whose temple is Reason.
E0899.body: Atwood brings in Isis of the old mythology to illustrate the divine beauty that is pursued. Isis is the Goddess whose temple is Reason [II.1 ¶50].

E0900.summary: In Olympiodorus, a figure for a condition above corporeal life and generation, the same as the Elysian Fields.
E0900.body: Olympiodorus is quoted here. The Islands of the Blessed stand for a condition above corporeal life and generation, just as “islands stand out of, as being higher than the sea” [II.4 ¶3]. He adds that “these are the same with the Elysian Fields” [II.4 ¶3].

E0901.summary: An unattributed saying that the adept then interprets.
E0901.body: An unattributed saying, “Man, it is said, was created of the dust of the earth” [I.3 n51], is cited and then interpreted by the adept.

E0902.summary: In Hermes, the ferment made from the gold of the wise with a fiery water; it tinges and fixes, and bodies cannot be made pure without it.
E0902.body:
Hermes is quoted here. Ixir is the ferment, made from the gold of the wise with a fiery water. It tinges and fixes, and it is that “without which bodies cannot be made pure” [I.3 n63].

Identities stated:
- gold and ferment: “gold, which is the ferment Ixir” [I.3 ¶58]
- Sericum: “we make of them Sericum, i.e., Ixir” [I.3 ¶59]
- seriacum: “we make seriacum, which is the ferment Ixir” [I.3 ¶62]
- Elixir, true Ferment: “This is the Elixir, Ixir, or true Ferment tinging and fixing” [I.3 n63]

E0903.summary: A Dutchman and elegant classical expositor of Hermetic matters; Atwood counts him in the golden chain of Hermetic philosophers.
E0903.body: Atwood calls Tollius a Dutchman and an elegant classical expositor on the same ground [I.1 ¶70]. His works listed are *Tollii Fortuita*, *Manudcutio ad Coelum Chemicum* and *Sapientia Insanies, sive Promissa Chemica* [I.1 n87]. Alongside Plato, Proclus, Porphyry, Faber and Michael Maier, he belongs to the “golden chain of Hermetic philosophers”. These writers traced the poets' allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil as their own, and Atwood cites them in support [III.1 ¶25].

E0904.summary: Cited in support of self-renunciation as the way to union.
E0904.body: Atwood cites words she attributes to Jacob in support of self-renunciation as the way to union: “Wherefore I abhor myself, cries Jacob” [IV.3 ¶58].

E0905.summary: Atwood holds that the Theurgic Art comes nearest to their doctrine of regeneration.
E0905.body: Atwood makes a comparison: the Theurgic Art comes nearest to “the perfect doctrine of regeneration preached by Jesus Christ and his apostles” [III.1 ¶11].

E0906.summary: The person who told Flammel the truth on this point.
E0906.body: The Jew is mentioned as the one who told Flammel the truth on this point [IV.3 ¶10].

E0907.summary: An author Atwood lists, with his works.
E0907.body: Beccher appears in a list of writers [I.1 ¶70]. His works given are *Physica Subterranea*, *Oedipus Chemicus Aperius Mysteria* and *Laboratorium Chemicum* [I.1 n86].

E0908.summary: Job and his book, cited often: his story is a type of the regenerate's sacrifice in faith, and his texts on Wisdom, Leviathan, gold and humbling support Atwood's argument.
E0908.body:
Atwood cites Job and the Book of Job often.

- **Job 28, on Wisdom.** Quoted at length to illustrate a contrast. Precious things hidden in the earth are brought to light, but the place of Wisdom is hidden from all living and known to God. For man, “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is Wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding” [III.1 ¶8, III.1 n5].
- **Job 41, Leviathan.** Quoted at length right after the account of how Typhon is subdued, with no commentary: “Canst thou draw out Leviathan with an hook?” [III.1 ¶63, III.1 n71].
- **Job 31 and 33.** Cited for the accountability of moral evil and the condemnation of trusting in gold: “If I have made gold my hope, or have said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence” [III.4 ¶7, III.4 ¶8, III.4 n5]. Note n6 goes with Adam hiding his iniquity in his bosom [III.4 n6].
- **Job 40:14.** Supports the humbling of the proud, followed by the promise of saving power: “THEN WILL I ALSO CONFESS UNTO THEE THAT THINE OWN RIGHT HAND CAN SAVE” [IV.3 ¶58, IV.3 n27]. The note marker follows the end of the quotation, and the text does not say how far back the citation reaches.
- **An objection answered.** The saying “no one by searching can find out the Almighty to perfection” holds, Atwood says, for a man searching by his own will. It does not hold for one conditionating in obedience to the Divine Will [IV.4 ¶23].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Job's story is “all a type” of the sacrifice in faith made by the Hermetically regenerated [APP ¶60]. His words illustrate the contrast between the perfection of the Law of Light and human defection: “I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now mine eye seeth Thee; therefore I abhor myself and repent in dust and ashes” [APP ¶90].

E0909.summary: Cited as a witness to Arnold's conversion of iron bars into gold at Rome.
E0909.body: Atwood cites John Andre as testifying that Arnold turned iron bars into gold at Rome [I.1 ¶43]. The source is *in addit. ad Speculum Rub de crim. Falsi*: “Nostris diebus habuimus magnum” [I.1 n52]. Our rendering, not the book's: In our days we had a great [one].

E0910.summary: Abbot of Westminster: a long-labouring seeker, misled by the adepts' enigmas, who found enlightenment by seeking Lully; his Testament supports the Lully story.
E0910.body: Atwood presents John Cremer, Abbot of Westminster, as an example. He laboured for a long time, was misled by the adepts' enigmas, and found enlightenment by seeking out Lully [I.1 ¶46]. His *Testament* (*Cremeri Testamentum*) supports the Lully story, and in it Cremer openly condemns the king's breach of faith [I.1 ¶47, I.1 n56].

E0911.summary: A practitioner who translated Sendivogius as The New Light of Alchemy, with a preface Atwood calls bold and striking.
E0911.body: Atwood names John French as a practitioner who translated Sendivogius (*The New Light of Alchemy*) and wrote a “bold and striking” preface [I.1 ¶71]. *French's Art of Distillation* is also cited [I.1 n90].

E0912.summary: Listed among the great spirits; Atwood names him as Agrippa's source for the means and principles of Occult Science.
E0912.body: Trithemius is listed among the great spirits [I.1 ¶39]. Atwood says that Abbot Trithemius was Agrippa's source for the means and principles of Occult Science [I.1 ¶64].

E0913.summary: The Emperor Julian, cited on vital rectification and on Divine union needing assistance; Atwood counts him among the Alexandrian revival figures.
E0913.body:
Julian is one of the Alexandrian revival figures (with Plotinus, Philo-Judaeus, Proclus, Porphyry, Jamblicus and Apuleius) who professed Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge and are quoted later [I.1 ¶27].

- From the *Oration to the Extra-Mundane Mother* (*Julian’s Orations II*), illustrating vital rectification: the purified soul receives Divine Light and strengthens its connate spirit, and disease comes from erroneous motion of the spirit. “health is a certain symmetry or equilibrium of nature” [IV.3 ¶30, IV.3 n10].
- The Emperor Julian's arguments, preserved by Cyril, support the view that Divine union needs such assistance: “without such assistance the Divine union is neither effected not rightly understood” [II.1 ¶52, II.1 n46].

E0914.summary: The Hebrew tradition Atwood cites in support at several points: Boehme's agreement with it, the Divine I Am, union with God as Fermentation, and going forth and returning.
E0914.body:
Atwood cites the Kabalah consistently in support:

- Boehme's testimony is said to agree “in all particulars with the most ancient Kabalah and profound experimental divinity” [III.2 ¶17].
- The Kabalah supports the view that in the Divine I Am is signified the Substant Unity of all that is [III.3 ¶79].
- Its union of man with God is identified with Fermentation: “that which in the Kabalah is denominated the union of man, reduced to the simplicity of the Monad, with God” [IV.3 ¶27].
- From *Sephir Jezirah*, cap. 1, going forth and returning, with closed-eye meditation, forms part of the final passage into accord: “Egredere et regredere, et propterea pactum praecisum est” [IV.3 ¶60, IV.3 ¶61, IV.3 n28]. Our rendering, not the book's: Go forth and return, and for this reason the covenant is cut.
- The Hebrew Kabbalah is described as “profound yet simple metaphysics”, “partially transmitted”, and agreeing within the same tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

E0915.summary: The Kabalistic commentators, medieval mystics and Rabbis, who Atwood says reached the same ideas as German metaphysics by ontological experiment.
E0915.body: Atwood cites these figures in support: they hold the same ideas as German metaphysics, but reached them by ontological experiment [III.2 ¶29].

E0916.summary: Cited, by way of Blackwell's Mythology, on creation as the Divine Will producing itself into material form.
E0916.body: Atwood cites the Kabalistic Interpreter (by way of *Blackwell’s Mythology*, letter 7) for creation as the Divine Will producing itself into form out of inane Identity: “the Divine Will, then alone operating, says the Kabalistic Interpreter, produces itself into a material form and recreation” [III.3 ¶43, III.3 n29].

E0917.summary: Kabalistic writers Atwood cites in support on the Quintessence, man as prototype, the Abyss as the Matter, uniting end and beginning, and the Law's hidden soul.
E0917.body:
Atwood cites the Kabalists in support at several points:

- They name the pure Quintessence “Lumen Vestimenti, the Vehicle of Light” [I.2 ¶16].
- They raise man up as containing the prototype of creation [II.1 ¶42].
- Their Abyss is identified with the Matter, “styled also by them Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite” [III.2 ¶60].
- From *Liber Jezirah*, cap. 1, the completed work unites end and beginning: “Unite the end to the beginning as the flame is united to the coal” [III.1 ¶50, III.1 n55].
- From the *Zohar*, part 3, fol. 152, verso, a view Atwood endorses: the Law's narrative clothes a sublime mystery, its Soul. “The story of the Law is the vestment of the Law” [III.3 ¶59, III.3 n39].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Kabalists celebrate the White Light as belonging to the Ancient of Days, the primeval Light [APP ¶157].

E0918.summary: Criticized by Atwood: his metaphysics stops short of objective realization and never got past the negative margin of intellectual intuition.
E0918.body: Atwood criticizes Kant together with Fichte and Schelling. Their metaphysics ends in void non-entity and skepticism and falls short of objective realization, though she ranks Schelling above the other two [III.2 ¶31]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Kant is criticized for never getting past the negative margin of intellectual intuition [APP ¶96]. He is also said to have “saw that”, but the text does not state what he saw. Apparently it is the preceding point about intellect and the Universal Reason [APP ¶117].
